text: The Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 under natural criteria (ix) and (x).
The Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve was designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1996.
The archipelago was designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2014 (site 'Archipel Bolama-Bijagós').
Three marine protected areas — João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park, Orango Islands National Park and the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area — were created in 2000 and 2005.
UNESCO identifies the archipelago as the second most important foraging area in Africa for migratory waterbirds of the East Atlantic Flyway, and as a sanctuary for a diversity of sharks and rays.
UNESCO attributes the property's exceptional state of conservation mainly to how the area is organised and to traditional resource management by local communities.
Sacred islands governed by customary rules act as refuges for biodiversity.
Overall management of the World Heritage property is coordinated by the Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas (IBAP).

BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project aims to establish a community marine protected area on the islands of Unhocomo and Unhocomozinho, recognised as sanctuaries for juvenile sea turtles (proposal, not yet designated).
Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025 as a natural property (“Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô”).
Agriculture, forest use, animal husbandry, fishing, shell gathering and ecological tourism are the main activities of island communities.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Shellfish are the principal source of animal protein for island communities.
Tourism in the archipelago has developed over recent decades but remains limited.
Created in 2000, Orango National Park is a core area of the Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve and is classified as IUCN Category II.
The archipelago, notably Orango, hosts hippopotamuses that live in seawater on an almost permanent basis — according to UNESCO, the only place in the world where the species does so.
Five of the world's seven sea turtle species frequent the park's beaches.
The park is also home to several monkey species, African manatees and several reptile species.
The park includes 33 villages with an estimated 3,369 inhabitants, mainly of the Bijagó ethnic group.

Activities in the park include farming (rice, oil palm and cashew), shellfish gathering, fishing and crafts.
A community guest house in the village of Anôr serves as a base for visitors to this part of Orango Island.

The park is described as the second most important green turtle (Chelonia mydas) nesting site in the South Atlantic.

The Rio Cacheu is not a river in the strict sense but a ria, where the sea reaches more than 150 km inland.
The region contains the Cacheu River mangroves, considered the largest continuous block of mangroves in West Africa.
Communities in and around the Cacheu park practise a sophisticated form of rice farming on mangrove soils, a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups (notably Felupe and Baiote).
Created in December 2000 by Decree-Law no. 12/2000 and managed by IBAP.
Wetland of International Importance (Ramsar site no. 2229) since 22 May 2015, with a listed area of 88,615 ha.
Its mangroves are considered the largest continuous mangrove block in West Africa; six mangrove species have been recorded.
The park's aims are to protect mangroves as the basis for fish reproduction, to conserve biodiversity and to improve living conditions of residents.
The mangroves provide food and refuge for protected or rare species such as the hippopotamus and the West African manatee, and serve as spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Each village in the site keeps one or more sacred forests, which act as reservoirs of biodiversity.

Besides rice fields, the mangrove provides fish, timber, honey, salt and traditional medicine.
Mangrove rice farming here is a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups and is described as unique cultural heritage.
Created by Decreto n.º 12/2000 (BO n.º 49, 4 December 2000).
According to the BioGuinea Foundation, the park was established in 2008 and covers 1,068 km². Other public records differ (see next fact), so the creation date and area are unconfirmed.
Wikidata records different values: inception in 1980 and in October 2007, and areas of 680 km² and 1,057.67 km².
Species listed by the BioGuinea Foundation include chimpanzees, Temminck's red colobus, baboons, roan antelope, waterbuck and buffalo.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Wetlands International reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.

At inscription, UNESCO assessed potential factors — pollution, fishing, navigation, infrastructure, oil exploration, tourism and climate change — as remaining at very low and/or distant levels.
Researchers describe the area as under increasing pressure from deforestation, future oil and gas prospection, tourism development, population growth, local and foreign fisheries, and pollution.
In 2014, offshore oil prospecting about 100 km north-west of the archipelago and a planned bauxite port on the Rio Grande de Buba were flagged as threats, both at project stage.
Overfishing by foreign fishermen is identified as the primary threat in a conservation project proposal for the archipelago.
Part of the motorised canoe fleet targets rays and sharks because of very high fin prices on Asian markets.
In Urok, Tiniguena reports new challenges from outside resource users who bring more predatory forms of exploitation.
The use of mangrove wood for smoking fish has repercussions on the environment.
UNESCO notes a strong likelihood that climate change will alter water circulation patterns and bring significant changes in sea level to this low-lying deltaic archipelago.
Sacred forests on the islands are described as threatened by exploitative tourism and natural resource extraction.
The expansion of cashew, encouraged by a monetarised economy, is reducing the preponderance of palm and rice.
Large areas of mangrove were converted to rice fields, many of which are abandoned after a few years as salt water intrudes and soils acidify.
Mangrove rice farming is declining for both climatic and social reasons.
Overexploitation of natural resources in the park includes fish, waterbirds and fuelwood.
On Dapack island, communities produced salt by boiling seawater over mangrove fuelwood before solar salt production was introduced.
Some migratory fish species have become rare through overfishing, and illegal fishing is practised mainly by non-resident fishers.
Wetlands International reports that park rangers' monitoring and surveillance have reduced illegal fishing and mangrove harvesting in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.
The park has been heavily degraded by slash-and-burn agriculture and overexploitation of natural resources.
The recent expansion of cashew plantations is a main threat to the dryland forests of the buffer zone.
In Guinea-Bissau's coastal mangrove villages, a shorter but more intense rainy season together with sea-level rise is making it harder for farmers to manage their rice fields.
Wetlands International reports that park rangers' monitoring and surveillance have reduced illegal fishing and mangrove harvesting in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.
The 2015 Ramsar description lists a phosphate mining industry, then at prospecting stage upstream on the Rio Cacheu, as a pressure from the surrounding region.
UNESCO identifies extensive agriculture, overfishing and mining as the reserve's main challenges.
GIZ reports that poverty and limited knowledge of sustainable land use lead local people to overuse the natural resources they depend on.
Citing Benin's national forest strategy, IUCN NL reports a 30% decrease in Mono Delta mangrove habitats since 1995, mainly from agricultural clearing, overfishing, logging and urbanisation.
For the overlapping Ramsar site 1017, Ramsar lists mangrove over-exploitation, logging-related soil erosion and coastal erosion as major threats.
IUCN's AGeReB project documents name the planned Adjarala hydroelectric dam upstream on the Mono River among pressures on the reserve.
The same document describes the coastal ecosystems of Ramsar site 1017 as heavily affected by large port and hydroelectric works.
Ramsar lists oil pollution, deforestation, overfishing, invasive species and urban expansion as pressures on the site.
In 2011 UNEP found that oil pollution had left mangroves in many intertidal creeks stripped of leaves and stems, with roots coated in a bitumen-like layer.
UNEP described the wetlands around Ogoniland as highly degraded and facing disintegration.
UNEP reported that fisheries suffer from destroyed mangrove fish habitat and persistent contamination of many creeks.
HYPREP's draft management framework names oil legacy impacts, livelihood dependence, tenure complexity and climate pressures as local realities.
UNEP found former mangrove areas reduced to bare ground being colonised by invasive species such as nipa palm.
HYPREP reports that its restoration teams are removing invasive nipa palms so native mangroves can recover.
A 2014 Rufford-funded project describes overgrazing, trampling and livestock faeces threatening the salt-collecting women's livelihoods and disturbing wildlife.
The same project reports that livestock faeces contaminate the water and the salt collected for sale.
Ramsar notes a need for regulation to prevent over-construction of tourist structures in the site.
The 2013 Ramsar information sheet warns that further tourism and housing construction nearby may harm the salt pans by increasing visitor numbers.
In 2012 the national environment authority lacked the personnel and finances to execute the site's management plan, according to a Rufford project record.
Since 2016 Maio's protected areas have been overseen by a small management unit within the island's agriculture and environment delegation.
The Ramsar sheet reports that overfishing in recent years, linked to strong immigration for the tourism industry, has considerably reduced fish stocks.
It notes that oceanographic researchers found the Aby lagoon in a state of generalised over-exploitation.
Harvesting plants for construction wood is described as a real threat to the survival of some species.
Locally, men supply firewood (essentially mangrove wood) and women smoke the fish.
In October 2026, residents near the park raised mangrove destruction and land sales with the park authority, according to the state news agency.
Ramsar lists timber exploitation, overfishing, uncontrolled tourism and hunting of birds and bats as threats.
Tourism inside the national park is not guided by clearly defined ecological principles.
The Ayamé I and II dams on the Bia river considerably affect the freshwater supply to the area.
Urbanisation and the gravel and sand extraction that accompanies it are a growing factor.
Ramsar notes that the site is threatened by sea erosion, pollution and excessive mangrove wood harvesting.
The 2023–2032 management plan reports mangroves often being harvested and not replanted, including for fish-smoking fuelwood.
The management plan describes fisheries as over-exploited, with fishers forced to use ever-smaller nets.
Blocked estuaries stop marine water and marine life from entering the lagoon.
Salt production once done on a small scale by community members has been taken over by large businesses, shutting some fishers out of local fishing areas.
Industrial aquaculture infrastructure has caused the loss of large tracts of mangrove in the Anloga restoration zone.
Severe coastal erosion has destroyed houses from Keta through Vodza to Kedzi.
The Akosombo dam is believed to have contributed to a major shortage of sediment in the lower Volta region.
The 2007 Ramsar sheet reports natural mangroves along the Gbaga falling from about 1,000 ha in 1999 to 546.97 ha in 2005.
Growing demand for firewood and charcoal accelerated vegetation loss in the Maritime Region.
A 2025 CTCN plan reports that women fish traders in three villages continue to cut mangroves despite reforestation by the WACA project.
The coast faces pronounced marine erosion at Agbodrafo, Kpémé and Aného.
The World Bank reports that Benin and Togo each lose about 15 metres of coastline a year, and 20 to 30 metres in some places.
The coastal lake and lagoon system is being progressively depleted by overfishing.
Deliberate poisoning of ponds and streams to catch fish is described as a common practice.
The Nangbéto dam, filled in 1987, changed the downstream water regime.
Invasive water hyacinth and water lettuce have spread in flooded areas.
Ramsar notes there is no management plan for the site.
UNESCO notes that fishing has considerably increased and that fishing gear, methods and target species have changed.
BACoMaB reports intensifying artisanal and coastal fishing around the park, with crews often non-Imraguen and sometimes targeting protected rays and sharks.
UNESCO links the main threats to unregulated development of maritime activities and coastal infrastructure.
It describes the risk of hydrocarbon pollution from the West African shipping route and the petroleum industry as considerable.
BACoMaB lists mining and oil exploration and exploitation in the area among pressures on the park.
BACoMaB reports that the park is exposed to sea-level rise, shoreline erosion and flooding of islands and villages.
UNESCO notes a permanent threat to the mangroves from the extension of rice cultivation and forest exploitation in the Fathala area.
In 2011 IUCN warned that low rainfall could raise salinity across the region and destroy the remaining mangroves.
UNESCO lists forest fires, excessive fishing, destruction of bird colonies and conflicts with industrial and agricultural development.
IUCN noted impacts from farming, fires, firewood gathering, pollution and possibly bird and turtle egg collection.
IUCN reports that the Pointe de Sangomar sand spit was breached in 1994 and the resulting island is moving progressively south.
IUCN judged resources insufficient to manage a protected area of this size.
It warned that unmanaged tourism could threaten natural values, particularly on the Île aux Oiseaux.
The World Heritage Committee asked for better waste and wastewater management to limit pollution.
The 2006 Ramsar sheet notes that the wetland's proximity to Banjul and its bisection by the highway give the land high development value.
The 2012 co-management plan reports settlements claiming land in the basin and blocked waterways increasing sedimentation of the mangroves.
The Ramsar sheet lists household waste dumping among threats.
Fertilisers, persistent pesticides and domestic and commercial waste are described as destructive to water quality.
The high cost of firewood in the urban area has led people to use mangrove as an alternative supply.
The 2012 plan highlights mangrove destruction and harvesting of juvenile oysters and cockles as major concerns.
Coastal erosion is rapidly altering the coastal strip and threatening infrastructure and habitat.
The Ramsar sheet cites inadequate enforcement of land-use and environmental law.
GRET reports particularly intensive exploitation of the Konkouré mangroves for firewood, salt production, rice parboiling and fish smoking.
The PROMAK project describes fuelwood cutting for domestic use, salt-making, fish smoking and rice parboiling as the main pressure.
Rice growing, market gardening and some destructive fishing techniques add to the degradation of the ecosystem.
PROMAK documents uncontrolled development linked to urban expansion, plastic pollution and inadequate sanitation.
The Garafiri hydropower scheme has altered local hydrology.
Few concrete measures have been implemented to protect the landscape; a protected area is now proposed, to be managed by the national parks office.

Sierra Leone's national auditors found land being sold and houses built along Aberdeen Creek, which is part of the estuary.
A news report describes unregulated structures at the creek destroying mangrove cover, and mangroves cut for firewood and land reclamation.
At the Targreen wetland, mangrove loss, sand mining and plastic and oil pollution were identified as the main threats to bird habitats.
The 2025 audit found that the protected-area authority's founding law does not mention wetlands, and that its operations are limited to protected areas.
Fish smoking around the lake relies predominantly on mangrove wood.
The 2007 Ramsar sheet records intensive fuelwood harvesting, sometimes in mangrove stands.
A Rufford-funded assessment reports continued mangrove harvesting for charcoal and firewood.
The Ramsar sheet records fishing with very small-mesh nets that remove the smallest fish.
A 2007 survey observed severe sand-mining pressure on the lake shore near Falie.
The Ramsar sheet records dumping of rotten fish and waste in the lake; a later grant record names plastics, old nets and manure as pollutants.
The Ramsar sheet records constant dry-season burning of savanna and bush, alongside farming and hunting.
Wetlands International introduced solar salt production on Dapack island (Cacheu) to replace boiling seawater with mangrove fuelwood.
The Restoration Initiative trained women on Elia Island in solar salt production, a less exhausting method that does not require cutting mangrove wood.
Elsewhere in Guinea-Bissau's coastal zone (Oio region), the DEDURAM project has offered women salt producers a solar technique since 2016.
Because the technique has already been introduced locally, a women-led solar salt enterprise is a plausible way to generate income while directly reducing fuelwood demand on mangroves.
In the village of Plindan (Cacheu), a fuelwood-efficient oven was installed to reduce fuelwood use for fish smoking, alongside a new women's association.
In the Bijagós, mangrove wood is used for smoking fish.
An earlier GEF-supported protected-areas project funded income-generating activities such as fish processing.
A fish-processing micro-enterprise built around fuel-efficient ovens could add value to artisanal catches while reducing mangrove cutting.
Women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River, have been trained in growing oysters by The Restoration Initiative.
The park's dense mangroves are spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Oyster cultivation creates income that depends on healthy mangroves, which could give communities a direct economic interest in protecting them.
Honey is among the services the Cacheu mangroves provide.

Wetlands International reports that the savings and loans groups it has set up in Guinea-Bissau since 2015 lend for activities including beekeeping, and describes a local beekeeper's mangrove-honey initiative (location within the country not stated).

A news report places beekeeping support within Wetlands International's project around the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, describing hives as 'mangrove guardians' because no one cuts a tree with an active hive.
A traceable mangrove-honey product could reward communities for keeping mangroves standing. Its commercial viability is unknown.
From 2015 to 2018, Wetlands International, IBAP and partners restored abandoned rice fields by breaching embankments and digging small channels to restore tidal flow.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Global Mangrove Watch publishes open mangrove-extent time series (CC BY 4.0) that could support baseline monitoring.
Results-based finance (e.g. carbon or biodiversity outcomes) for community-led restoration of abandoned rice fields could be explored, building on — not duplicating — the existing REDD+ project.
Ecological tourism is already one of the main activities of island communities.
A community guest house in Anôr village serves visitors to Orango.
Sacred forests are described as threatened by exploitative tourism.
Tourism that is community-owned and respects customary rules could add income while steering away from the exploitative forms identified as a threat.
The Urok community MPA is managed directly by local communities and aims to secure their access to prime fishing grounds.
BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project targets sustainable marine resource management and improved livelihoods in the archipelago's MPAs.
Traceable products from community-managed grounds (for example processed shellfish or fish) could link conservation outcomes to income, if harvest limits are respected.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Cashew expansion is reducing the preponderance of palm and rice.
Adding value to products from existing natural palm groves could make traditional agroforestry more competitive with cashew expansion.

IUCN NL and Eco-Benin are working to preserve mangroves in the Bouche du Roy reserve and surroundings, financed by blue carbon credits; planned work includes nurseries, village-led planting and alternative income, especially for women.
Eco-Benin reports more than 500 hectares planted and areas made sacred through traditional sacralisation practices in the Bouche du Roy (self-reported).
Community-run mangrove nurseries and paid restoration work are a plausible regenerative activity here, because an existing blue-carbon project already plans nurseries and alternative income.
UNESCO reports that since the reserve was created, projects have promoted ecotourism, particularly whale and dolphin watching.
The EU-funded AGeReB action (2023–2027), run by IUCN, IUCN NL and Eco-Benin, includes support for the Nonvignon tourism training centre.
Locally owned guiding and ecotourism services could offer income that depends on a healthy delta, as an alternative to resource overuse.
HYPREP's 'Mangrove Vanguards' programme trains young people and women to run mangrove nurseries, and requires restoration contractors to buy their seedlings.
HYPREP reports completing a first phase of mangrove restoration covering 560 ha and starting a second phase of 438 ha across seven communities (self-reported).
Because restoration contractors already buy community-grown seedlings, nursery enterprises are a defensible regenerative activity here, if demand continues beyond the current phases.
The 2013 Ramsar information sheet reports that more than 70 women derived their livelihood from salt extraction, an activity it describes as sustainable.
In 2012 the women's salt cooperative produced little salt and lost its traditional market, according to the grantee report.
Livestock faeces contaminate the salt collected for sale.
Keeping livestock out of the salt pans and marketing a cleaner, traceable traditional salt could strengthen the women's income while keeping the site in use. Market demand is unknown.

In October 2020 the national parks office (OIPR) and the World Bank-financed WACA project signed an agreement to develop and restore mangrove ecosystems in the Azagny and Îles Ehotilé parks (news report).
A local management committee coordinated by OIPR promotes participatory management with the park's neighbouring communities.
Community-run nurseries and paid restoration work could build on this agreement and on the existing local committee, if restoration funding continues.
Locally, men supply mangrove firewood and women smoke the fish.
In Guinea-Bissau, a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven was installed in Plindan (Cacheu) to reduce fuelwood use.
Fuel-efficient ovens run by women processors could reduce mangrove wood demand here too. No such initiative was found for this site.

A Rocha Ghana, with the Wildlife Division, reports planting 20 ha of degraded mangrove, establishing a woodlot and training community trainers in sustainable mangrove harvesting in four communities (2021–2023, self-reported).
The management plan describes a traditional cycle of planting and harvesting mangroves along the lower Volta creeks at Anyanui.
The Wildlife Division has established a tree nursery that distributes seedlings to surrounding communities.
Managed mangrove woodlots supplying fish-smoking fuelwood could relieve pressure on natural stands, building on local practice and recent project work.
The Wildlife Division is trying to promote bird watching and night turtle walks.
Community guiding services could share in this tourism and give residents an income linked to protecting nesting beaches and bird areas.
A 2025 CTCN technical-assistance plan, requested by a women fish traders' group at Togokomé, proposes replanting mangroves and solar fish smoking and cold storage (planned, not yet implemented).
The World Bank reports that 257 hectares of mangroves have been planted in Togo under the WACA programme.
Because women fish traders still cut mangroves for fuel, combining replanting with solar fish preservation addresses a documented cause of loss.
Since 2000 IUCN, the park, IFAD and FIBA have supported Imraguen women with processing facilities, hygiene and management training and new packaging for traditional products.
Inside the park only the Imraguen may fish, on foot or from sailing boats; motorised boats are banned.
Traceable traditional products tied to sail-only fishing could raise income per catch rather than catch volume, in line with the park's fishing rules.
UNESCO reports that grass-roots village associations run mangrove nurseries and reforestation plots.
A women's group in the delta has led mangrove reforestation since 2007 and set harvesting periods and biological rest periods (news report).
FAO reports training women seafood processors at Niodior in food safety, hygiene and entrepreneurship.
Women-led shellfish processing tied to harvest rules and mangrove replanting builds on documented local practice.
The Bamboung bolon became a community marine protected area in 2003, proposed and led by the Senegalese NGO Océanium with funding from the French Global Environment Facility.
IRD monitored its fish populations between 2003 and 2012.
Products or services linked to community-managed fishing areas could reward their protection. Viability and current status are unknown.
The Gambia designated the TRY Association with exclusive use rights to the cockle and oyster fishery in the Tanbi special management area.
TRY members agreed to extend the closed season to nine months to let oysters grow bigger.
A 2010 grant set up microcredit for members, who learned to pickle oysters for sale during the closed season.
TRY received a GEF grant through the National Environment Agency for mangrove reforestation and aquaculture.
Value-added oyster products sold under existing co-management rights could raise income without increasing harvest.
Guinée Écologie reports supporting ten women's groups with solar tarpaulins and technical help in the Konkouré delta and the Mélakoré estuary in 2025.
BirdLife reports a CEPF-funded pilot in Dubréka prefecture producing salt with sunlight and tarpaulins instead of fuelwood.
Since salt boiling is a documented driver of mangrove cutting here, women-led solar salt production is a defensible regenerative activity.
Guinée Écologie reports supporting 98 women in the Konkouré delta in 2025 to rebuild and use improved fish-smoking ovens.
Wider use of improved ovens could cut the fuelwood demand that drives mangrove cutting here.
Guinée Écologie installed oyster garlands at pilot sites, two of them in the Konkouré delta, in 2025.
PROMAK describes honey as a little-developed value chain in the Konkouré landscape, with a few pilot initiatives, and commissioned a 2026 market and value-chain study.
Oyster and honey products depend on healthy mangroves, so value chains built around them could reward protection, subject to the planned market study.
Freetown City Council reports planting 275,000 mangroves in three coastal communities, tracked digitally by community youth; whether these sites lie in the Ramsar site is not established.
A blue-carbon developer announced in May 2024 a conservation and restoration project covering 10,000 hectares of the estuary; its current status is unknown.
Community nurseries and paid planting could supply restoration in the estuary, if a restoration or carbon project proceeds.
In December 2024 the Sierra Leone Nature Guide Association trained stakeholders, youths and pupils around the Targreen wetland, part of the estuary, in bird conservation.
Trained local guides could offer birdwatching services that give residents an income linked to protecting bird habitat.
Wetlands International Africa supported the production and use of improved stoves with women in Fallie and Senbehun, and a cassava processing unit in Teh, under an EU-funded mangrove project (2025).
The 2007 Ramsar sheet records earlier trials of fish-smoking structures and a solar fish drier.
Locally made improved stoves and smokers could reduce demand for mangrove wood, the main fuel for fish smoking here.
A 2016–2017 small grant trained fishers in selective fishing, supplied approved net sizes and started cage fish farming on the lake (marked completed; no outcome data).
Legal-mesh fishing combined with small-scale fish farming could reduce pressure on juvenile fish while sustaining income.

Created in 2004 to protect and manage Guinea-Bissau's biodiversity through the National System of Protected Areas, which covers about 26% of the national territory. It coordinates management of the Bijagós World Heritage property and manages the Cacheu park. Its 2006 annual report records the appointment of wardens for the Orango, João Vieira–Poilão and Cacheu parks; current park-level arrangements were not re-verified.

Conservation trust fund established in 2011 as a long-term financing mechanism for Guinea-Bissau's protected areas, with funding channelled through IBAP. It supports Orango National Park, runs the Blue Bijagós project and runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. It is listed as a member of the Consortium of African Funds for the Environment (CAFÉ).

text: Guinean NGO that supported the creation and participatory governance of the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area.

With IBAP and partners, ran a 2015–2018 initiative to conserve and restore the Cacheu mangroves, including ecological restoration of abandoned rice fields, solar salt and a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven. It reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. In Liberia's Lake Piso reserve it has supported improved stoves and a cassava processing unit under an EU-funded mangrove project.
Provided technical assistance to the coastal planning that led to the 1996 Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve.

Restoration programme uniting 10 countries and three Global Environment Facility agencies (IUCN, FAO and UNEP). Its Guinea-Bissau project works with women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River. The reviewed source does not say which agency leads the Guinea-Bissau project.

Regional coalition for the conservation and sustainable management of West Africa's coastal and marine areas. It partners with Rainforest Trust on a proposed project supporting new marine protected area designations in the Bijagós.
Raising funds, with PRCM, to support government designation of four new marine protected areas in the Bijagós, including three island community MPAs (proposed project).
National NGO supporting a network of environmental schools (EVA) around the park.
Runs a research project on the ecological integrity of the Bijagós as a key site for waders on the East Atlantic Flyway, with partners including Tiniguena.
Benin's national wildlife-reserve agency; supervising administration of the Bouche du Roy marine protected area inside the reserve.
Implemented the 2013–2019 project, funded by the German International Climate Initiative, that prepared the transboundary biosphere reserve.
Worked with local partners, GIZ and both governments to create the reserve, and partners Eco-Benin on blue-carbon mangrove work.
Beninese NGO running mangrove restoration and sacralisation and a blue-carbon project in the Bouche du Roy area of the reserve.
Federal agency under the Ministry of Environment carrying out the Ogoniland clean-up, mangrove restoration and livelihood programmes, and preparing the Ramsar site management plan.
Carried out the 2011 independent environmental assessment of Ogoniland whose recommendations frame the clean-up.
Maio NGO that managed the Salinas under a 2012 delegation, monitors its birds and turtles, and leads co-management of Maio's protected areas.
National environment directorate with the mandate and authority on biodiversity and conservation in Cabo Verde.
Holds delegated management of the national-park part of the Ramsar site.
World Bank-financed coastal resilience programme; funded mangrove restoration with OIPR in Côte d'Ivoire and mangrove planting in Togo.
Management authority of the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site, mandated to enforce the law.
Ran the 2021–2023 PAPBio mangrove restoration and livelihoods project in four Keta Lagoon communities, with the Wildlife Division.
Its staff act against unsustainable logging, fishing and illegal hunting at the site; it is the implementing agency of WACA in Togo.
UNFCCC technology body that prepared a 2025 technical-assistance plan for women-led mangrove restoration and solar fish preservation in Togo's Maritime Region.
Public administrative body that manages the park under its own law (2000-024).
Conservation trust fund created in 2009 that provides long-term funding for the park, including sea surveillance and shared governance.
Named as the park's managing body in the 1993 Ramsar sheet; UNESCO names it as a partner in integrated management planning.
Senegalese marine conservation association that proposed and led the Bamboung community marine protected area project.
Community-based non-profit founded in 2007 that holds exclusive cockle and oyster use rights in Tanbi; it received the Equator Prize in 2012.
Has managed the Tanbi Wetlands Complex since 2005 and assists with enforcement under the shellfish co-management plan.
Implemented the USAID Ba Nafaa project, with WWF, that supported the Tanbi shellfish co-management plan.
Guinean NGO running mangrove restoration, solar salt, improved ovens and oyster pilots in the Konkouré delta, and a partner in the PROMAK protected-area project.
Leads the EU-funded PROMAK consortium (2025–2028) working towards legal protection of the Konkouré mangroves.
Named as the future manager of the protected area proposed for the Konkouré mangroves.
Statutory protected-area authority; carries out enforcement against encroachment at the estuary, though its mandate over wetlands is limited.
Runs mangrove planting in Freetown coastal communities under its #FreetownTheTreeTown campaign.
Ran bird-conservation and nature-guiding training around the Targreen wetland in 2024.
National authority for conservation forestry; lists the Lake Piso Multiple Sustainable Use Reserve among Liberia's protected areas.
Named in the 2007 Ramsar sheet as the agency responsible for the Lake Piso wetland.
Grantee of a 2016–2017 GEF small-grant project on sustainable fishing at Lake Piso.
